result.summary: For the MCAP sink, repeated maintenance timeouts drive nonblocking I/O completion polling independently of flush deadlines.
result.applicability: The production worker repeatedly calls recv_timeout(interval), then invokes Recording::tick after each timeout. That tick unconditionally drives asynchronous I/O completion processing.
result.exception_analysis: Configured flushing and aged-batch flushing are permitted deadline work. However, McapCore::poll calls writer.progress(false) before checking the batch deadline and again afterward. Those calls submit without waiting and inspect the completion queue regardless of whether a deadline is due. This is completion processing, not observational sampling or pacing. The API's description of polling as optional does not establish an exception to the rule.
result.counterevidence: Packet arrival is channel-signaled, and disconnection exits the worker. Dora and OTEL inherit a no-op tick. MCAP ticking also performs legitimate timed flushing, and explicit flush barriers block on kernel completion. These narrow the violation to the independent completion polling performed by maintenance ticks.

finding.trigger: An MCAP sink remains connected while the packet channel is idle, including while accepted I/O awaits completion.
finding.expected: Use explicit completion notifications for asynchronous I/O progress; reserve timed wakeups for the operations' actual deadlines.
finding.observed: Each maintenance timeout invokes tick, which calls writer.poll and unconditionally performs nonblocking submission and completion-queue inspection.
finding.impact: Idle workers repeatedly wake and inspect I/O state even when no flush deadline is due. Between submissions or barriers, completion retirement and failure observation depend on subsequent maintenance ticks rather than completion notifications.
